_about: Hard Hat Mack, Electronic Arts, 1983. A 42,112-byte .COM, rebuilt
byte-identically, with all 22,393 bytes of its code region read.
It is not 8086 code somebody wrote. It is 6502 code a program translated,
instruction by instruction, off the Apple II original. 93% of every `cmp`
is followed by `cmc`, because the 6502's carry means the opposite of the
8086's; `mov al, X / inc al / dec al` appears 511 times, because LDA sets
flags and mov does not; AL appears in half of all instructions and there is
no 16-bit arithmetic anywhere, because the 6502 has one 8-bit accumulator;
and there is not a single register push in 9,062 instructions. The three
other games in this repository score zero on every one of those markers.
Read AL as the accumulator, BL and CL as X and Y, and the program stops
looking strange. The toolkit's knowledge/14-translated-binaries.md has the
measurements.
That is why probelib.py found 0 of 250 entry points: there was never a C
compiler. It is why 221 call targets exist for perhaps eighty behaviours:
one per JSR target. It is why 436 variables sit in 132 clusters between the
routines that own them. And it is why the drawing is what it is -- a 200-word
scanline table because the Apple II hi-res screen is interleaved, a one-pixel
XOR plotter, and a turtle-graphics interpreter at 0x1A7E that is Applesoft's
shape-table mechanism carried across.
The game has one bit of audio and plays a three-octave equal-tempered scale
on it. music_tick advances a 16-bit phase accumulator 0x78 times a call and
toggles port 0x61 against a duty threshold that drifts by 4 every sample:
pulse-width modulation. Solve for the rate that puts note 19 on A440 and you
get 6,992 samples a second, so the game was written expecting 58.27 frames a
second -- at which note 0 lands on 146.81 Hz against D3's 146.83.
tools/decode-sound.py reproduces all of it.
Five names in an earlier version were wrong, all guessed from caller counts.
Six bracketed constants are not addresses at all; see _not_addresses.

its two neighbours, and 0x04952. NASM re-emits them as the same bytes, so
the rebuild is unaffected, but `and bx, word [0x1e]` is a coincidence of

This is the mirror of the residue problem knowledge/11 records. There the
question was whether unreached bytes are code; here it is whether reached
bytes that decode are data. Both are answered by what refers to them, and
